utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Judge Nosworthy is absent this morning for urgent personal reasons; we've decided to continue in her absence, and she does, in fact, hope to join us later in the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Jelic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The cross-examination by Ms. Kravetz will continue in a moment. Please bear in mind, as I said to you yesterday morning, that the solemn declaration to speak the truth continues to apply to your evidence. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yesterday when we left off we were speaking about your meetings with the chief of the Urosevac SUP. You had told us that the chief of the Urosevac SUP during the war was Mr. Janicevic, Colonel Janicevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Colonel Janicevic was the chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Was he later replaced by Colonel Bozidar Filic?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sometime in the middle of the war he was replaced by Colonel Filic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you had interactions and meetings with both of these men, correct?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the periods when they were chiefs, I was in contact with them and attended meetings with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now, when you received an order from your superior commander to carry out a joint action with a PJP detachment, a MUP unit, would you coordinate the implementation of such an action with the chief of the Urosevac SUP?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if we would receive a plan for the execution of an anti-terrorist action, then we would have a coordinating meeting and agree on that meeting how to implement the task.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And I take it the situation would be the same in the event that you received an order to carry out a joint operation involving the JSO or the SAJ, you would also coordinate the implementation of such action with the chief of the Urosevac SUP?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We received tasks, and in parallel SUP would receive their tasks. And only when the chief of the SUP receives a task and I have already received mine, he would call me or I would call him, depending on who received it earlier, and then we would organize a coordination of that task.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And at these meetings, at these coordination meetings, what sort of information was exchanged between you and the personnel from the Urosevac SUP?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, we would exchange basic information about the enemy, the terrorist forces, their strength, location, where they were, and the rest would be coordinating through the documents that we received, I from the corps and he from his staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: He would also - "he," meaning the chief of the SUP of Urosevac - would also give you information about actions that the MUP was carrying out on their own in our area of responsibility, correct?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The area of responsibility - I have to clarify this - the area of responsibility of my brigade was the territory I described a few days ago; however, the area of responsibility of the brigade was where the brigades were deployed, where the units of the brigade were deployed, not the rest of the territory. So it was mostly I who gave him information about where my units were deployed, and he would give me information of the actual deployment because his possibilities of observation were greater on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: He would also give you information about actions, large-scale anti-terrorist actions that the MUP was going to carry out on its own without the involvement of the VJ; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he executed an action without the participation or support of the army, then he would just provide me information that was relevant to me, whether there were any military installations in the vicinity, whether some unit was deployed in the areas, lest that unit take some action that would lead to a clash between the army and the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So this information would be exchanged prior to the carrying out of these actions by the MUP?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, we exchanged information, if an action was planned, before the plan was executed, before the anti-terrorist action was executed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, General. You described your contacts with the chief of the SUP in Urosevac as very professional. During your meetings, your regular meetings, with either of Mr. Janicevic or Mr. Filic, did they at any moment, either of these two men, raise any sort of concerns or complaints regarding the behaviour or misconduct of VJ units on the ground?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. The information we exchanged at those meetings would include -- for instance, if they encountered inappropriate conduct by commanding officers or soldiers, something that disrupted law and order, they would provide me with that information. And more specifically, their professional, their technical service in charge of that would provide that information to my security organ.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did Colonel Janicevic at any time during -- at these meetings raise any concerns about the VJ committing crimes against the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While he was chief of the Urosevac SUP, he never shared such information with me, except for misdemeanours. He never told me about any major criminal offences.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We have heard evidence in this case, General, about complaints raised by Colonel Janicevic with the MUP staff, basically complaints regarding criminal behaviour, improper behaviour of VJ units on the ground and an allegation that most of the crimes on the ground were being committed by the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This, Your Honours, is Exhibit P1996, it's the minutes of the MUP staff meeting, 7th May 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did Colonel Janicevic at any moment complain to you that most of the crimes on the ground were being committed by VJ units?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He never told me any such thing. He told me about individual cases that happened, but never any major crimes, serious crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The minutes of the same MUP staff meeting that I just referred to on 7th May records Colonel Filic complaining about incomprehensible behaviour from the part of the VJ, and he says that soldiers are being detained for looting but that the VJ's not taking sufficient measures against these soldiers. Were you aware that such a problem existed within your units?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me first answer the first part of the question concerning Janicevic, he was not chief of Urosevac SUP at the time, and at the time it happened in Pristina, he was talking about Pristina and I was in Urosevac. So those crimes, if they really happened, he was talking about the locality he was in charge of then, that's the town of Pristina and its broader area, not that 243rd Brigade and not Urosevac. So I can't tell you more about it. It was not my territory, and Urosevac was no longer his responsibility. As for Mr. Filic, he never told me about any serious crimes. He did share with me information about minor problems and that was dealt with through his operatives and my organs of security and military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see my colleague Mr. Ivetic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have to intervene because the question -- two questions ago referred to Mr. Janicevic and some alleged comments in the minutes. I've just now been able to open the minutes and read them. Those comments where not in the minutes at all. So I would ask that counsel please cite exactly to where the foundation or basis is for these questions if she's going to imply that things are in evidence, when, in fact, they are not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, we ask look at the document. I was just trying to proceed without having to refer to the document. It's P1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, let's have the relevant passage on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: It's page 5 of the English and 4 of the B/C/S. The passage I was referring to is somewhere in the middle of the page of the English. It starts with: "The military is not taking sufficient measures and most crimes are being perpetrated by the VJ ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And this is who speaking?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This is Colonel Janicevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you maintaining your objection, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Indeed. It's in Pristina. She's talking about Urosevac with the General who was in Urosevac in Pristina. She's mixing apples and oranges. In the Serbian they're talking about regular crimes. They're not talking about crimes in actions. They're talking about crimes that have been described in the document which are looting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That wasn't the basis for your objection as I understood it. The witness has already explained that and he has endeavoured to correct the misrepresentation which he claims was made by counsel, but there was nothing improper in it. People do make mistakes if that's what's happened. Your tone of righteous indignation was hardly justified in the circumstances. Can we go back please to the previous page. Is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I think you want page 4 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Page 4, thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, my question was simply whether Colonel Janicevic during his tenure as chief of the SUP in Urosevac had raised these concerns which are being expressed here at this meeting. I am well aware that he was chief of Pristina SUP at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, with your leave, Your Honour, just technical issue, could we have the same page in B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The reason I wanted to see it was just to see the description of Janicevic on the page, and it is chief of the SUP in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: May I move on, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: General, last Friday you told us that to your knowledge there were no crimes committed by members of your brigade and that all crimes that were discovered were prosecuted. What type of crimes were you referring to when you said that all crimes that were discovered were prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This is, Your Honours, at page 18955 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The most serious crimes, that is, murders, were not committed by any members of the army, so no such were charged. Most crimes were looting and robbery and theft, and all of those were detected, criminal reports were filed, and the persons were tried.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how many cases were prosecuted? We're talking about members of your brigade.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that 15 to 20 serious crimes were processed and between 40 and 50 less serious ones.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And when you say "less serious ones," exactly which sort of crimes are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, regular theft, breaking and entering into small shops, businesses, grocery stores, that kind of thing. There were also breaches of discipline, going absent without official leave, failure to carry out a task, all that was processed, tried, dealt with before a military court.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that most of the crimes that were prosecuted were crimes committed against the VJ, they weren't crimes against the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you the ratio at this moment, but regardless of whether it was a crime against the army or members of the army or against civilians, it was always prosecuted. No distinction was made in that sense between crimes committed against civilians and crimes committed against members of the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: General, during the course of combat actions when a VJ officer observed a member of the MUP committing a crime - and by that I mean a crime against a civilian - what action would that VJ officer take? Was he able to stop that crime, arrest the MUP officer? What sort of measure could he take?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anyone who tries to perpetrate a criminal offence and is seen by someone else, if that someone else is a member of the army or a regular civilian, it is his duty to try to prevent it. If he's not able to prevent it, he has to report it to our security organ, we inform the SUP, and the SUP then takes measures against such a policeman. If one of them was trying to commit a crime, it is certain that he cannot be prevented in it by two or three people even, let alone a single person, because the person -- the one trying to commit a crime is armed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You said the person, it was his duty to try to prevent it, the duty of the officer. Is this a legal duty of a VJ officer when he observes someone, a MUP -- member of the MUP or another civilian, committing a crime, does he have a legal duty to prevent it and to take measures?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He has a legal duty to prevent if he's able to prevent. For instance, hypothetically speaking, if I am somewhere where somebody's trying to commit a crime and I am alone while two or three of them are together trying to commit that crime, I am physically incapable of preventing it. I can issue a warning; if they listen to me, fine, if not, I take immediate steps to report to my superiors, to the security organs, and they inform the MUP, and the MUP then organize pursuit, roadblocks, does everything to apprehend them. It all depends on where the officer is in the chain of command. If he's part of a platoon of a military police and his command is close by, he will certainly take measures to stop it there and then, but if you are alone and you have no way of stopping it, it it's a different situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, I understand the example you're giving, if the VJ officer is alone. I was asking precisely if the VJ officer is with his unit and is taking part in a combat action together with members of the MUP and he observes, for example, a MUP -- a member of the MUP attacking and beating a civilian, is he -- does he have the legal duty to arrest that person and take him away from -- back to the SUP, for example?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he's in an area of combat action, he cannot know whether the person being beaten is a civilian or a terrorist, especially if they are at a distance of 50 to 100 metres away. If they are right there in front of him, then of course it is his duty to grab the civilian away from the policeman and protect them from the beating. It all depends on the situation. It's not the same thing if he was there in the first place or if he has just walked in on that scene. If all that is happening at a distance, he cannot know whether the person being beaten is a terrorist who had just illegally crossed the border, what he had been doing before that, and what the policeman is doing, what he is reacting to. We can only speculate. At any rate, all the serious crimes, murders, rapes, and such have to be prevented, regardless of the situation and the circumstances. But you certainly know from your experience, even better than I do, that all sorts of crimes take place and each one is very specific, happens under specific circumstances. I'm trying to speak in general terms, though.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, I understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry to intervene. Sorry, General, to bother you with this query. I appreciate what you have just said, that's a good spirit. But when we saw one of your answers you said that nobody shared with you the information about serious crimes attributed to the VJ, but you were told about the minor crimes or misdemeanours. Why was that information kept away from you or why didn't you ask for it? It would become well-known that this has happened because a serious crime has an impact, there's a news about it. Why was that kept away from you? I mean, I couldn't understand that. I'm sorry to bother you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm certain that my security organs and organs of the military police had almost the same or identical information that they exchanged with the SUP, and the SUP is the professional agency in charge. With the SUP, we never discussed any specific cases if somebody committed a misdemeanour, stole a vehicle. We discussed what we should plan, what we should do in the forthcoming period, and we would discuss very serious crimes if any happened in the area of responsibility. In our reports that we received, we did not see any serious crimes committed by members of the VJ. Whether the SUP had any such information that they kept away from us, I really cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Going back to your previous answer, you said that when a crime is committed right in front of the officer, the officer of course has the duty to grab the civilian, take it away from the perpetrator. In -- and I understand what you're saying, that it's always not clear whether the victim is a civilian or not when you're engaged in combat. But if the person is clearly a civilian and the VJ officer witnesses this crime, what measures can that VJ officer take vis-a-vis the perpetrator? For example, can he arrest him on the spot?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he's in an area of combat action, then the person committing a crime is immediately arrested. So the answer to your question is: Yes, he can arrest him immediately if that is a serious crime. If the person trying to commit a crime is a member of the VJ, he's taken away to pre-trial custody. If he's a member of the MUP, then he's taken to the MUP. But that's a hypothetical case. We never had mixed units where a policeman would be next to a military policeman or a VJ member. So all I'm saying is speculation, what would happen if it --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. We're talking about a hypothetical case. Thank you, General. I want to move on to a different topic now about Racak. Yesterday -- well, and on Friday you discussed the operation conducted by the MUP in Racak, and you were shown a report signed by you, I think it's Exhibit 5D1377, that you sent to the Pristina Corps command dated 17th January 1999. Now, in your report you say that part of a combat group that was deployed in the Stimlje area was conducting a training exercise on 15th January, the day the Racak operation took place. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Part of the unit was undergoing combat training along those routes, it is a reinforced platoon. They were training, and that unit, in addition to their basic task, was supposed to prevent spillover of terrorists from the Jezerska Planina to the Lipovacka Planina but in addition to that to provide security along the Stimlje-Suva Reka road and they were carrying out training. That group was up there in accordance with the agreement, namely it was supposed to be about 150 men.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I see my colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that the question put by my learned friend is a bit imprecise. I think that the witness spoke very specifically, not Stimlje but Dulje. Let's see what the witness says. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The training took place at Dulje, and as far as I can see here, if it can be enlarged a bit, please. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you go on, the witness was dealing with the matter, he's able to explain himself clearly, and matters such as the one you've just raised, Mr. Cepic, can be dealt with in re-examination. Please continue, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: General, you had been informed by the chief of the Urosevac SUP that the Racak -- that the MUP was going to conduct an anti-terrorist operation in Racak on 15th January; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct. He called me to his staff and informed me that he had had approval for this plan of anti-terrorist action, in view of the terrorists who had lethally wounded his policemen on the Stimlje-Urosevac road a few days before that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You said that your unit had been -- was deployed there in Dulje heights and had been deployed there for several weeks prior to this incident in Racak on 15 January; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your statement is only partially correct, not several weeks. That unit was there from April 1998, from April 1998, and it had not moved from that area. According to the agreement, it was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: But only a part of the combat group that was authorised to -- whose deployment was authorised in Dulje heights was taking part in this combat exercise, training exercise, that you describe in your report. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please, let me explain this. This is one combat group with a command at the Dulje pass. It is a reinforced company; according to the agreement, it's about 150 men. That combat group, we call it number 1, was in two localities, located in two different places, in the upper part, at the Dulje pass where the command was, and that is where training took place. The other locality is near Canovica Brdo so not in Stimlje, by the road going from Stimlje to Dulje and Suva Reka there is the smaller part of that combat group. Within that combat group there was a subgroup, if we can call it that conditionally speaking, that is a mobile unit which secured military transports, columns, provided physical security for them from Stimlje to Suva Reka and back. If one group would go escorting the column, if another group came, from this group, from Canovica Brdo that is to say the smaller group, immediately two or three combat vehicles with wheels go and accompany the next group.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. You've explained that during your testimony. I wanted to know what was the location of this particular group that was carrying out a training exercise. They were in the vicinity of Racak, weren't they, General?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The training exercise was being carried out by the combat group in Dulje, where the command was. They were carrying out tactical exercises from squad level up to platoon level, perhaps up to company level. That is where this organized training took place; otherwise, in principle, in the army there is incessant training with equipment, but that is where the training exercise was taking place, in the area of Dulje, not the village of Dulje, but Dulje pass - that is to say in the mountains of Dulje.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And this sort of training exercise had been authorised by you? You were aware that it was taking place?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. Training takes place in a planned fashion. The commanding officers have their own schedule, and all the training exercises have to be approved and they were approved.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: But prior to conducting or giving the authorisation for this training exercise, you did not notify the KVM, did you, General, that your unit was going to be conducting a training exercise that morning, the 15th January?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The training that takes place in three -- in up to three vehicles were not supposed to be notified or announced, whereas larger-scale exercises had to be announced.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: General, we had the testimony in this court of General Maisonneuve from the KVM, and he clearly stated that this deployment of your group that was conducting this training exercise was an unauthorised [Realtime transcript read in error "authorised"] deployment out of barracks. Would you agree with General Maisonneuve?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree with General Maisonneuve at all because we have approval in writing as to where this unit is, then practically I was deceived by the corps command and the corps command was deceived by the army commander, perhaps the General Staff even. Furthermore, I think that that unit at Dulje was visited at least ten times, and never ever were there any critical remarks made -- or perhaps at the outset it was too big, but then when it was reduced to allowed levels, then the gentleman from this commission even counted the soldiers and the pieces of equipment there. So that's where the only problem was, and this went on for, say, about ten days or so. From that moment onwards, there were no problems with that unit, especially not in terms of their personnel levels, equipment levels, armament levels, not even Mr. Maisonneuve personally. I don't see how he can now say that they were at an unlawful level. Had this been unlawful, he would have been protesting and there would have been a reaction, but this unit was up there, as I said, in continuity from April 1998 onwards involving different compositions, sometimes bigger, sometimes smaller.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you recall that General Maisonneuve met on the day after the Racak incident occurred on 16th January with a liaison officer from your brigade? Do you recall that, Colonel Petrovic, and the records of that meeting --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This is, Your Honours, Exhibit 1771.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: -- clearly indicate General Maisonneuve complaining that this was an unauthorised deployment out of barracks.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a small correction straight away. Petrovic is a lieutenant-colonel, not a general. He was assigned from my unit to be involved in cooperation with the mission. It would be a good thing if we had a look at the document itself; however, I'm telling you. That unit was inspected so often that it is simply inexplicable to hear that now, how come is that unit there. You have the documents, I don't really. What units were supposed to be engaged in protection. I know that there were three in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, not taking into account the in-depth security ones. Lapusnik, Volujac, and Dulje were the groups that were assigned.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Can we have a look --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you move on, in line 9 of page 16, the word should be unauthorised, not authorised. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Can we have Exhibit 1771 on the screen. I think this is the incorrect exhibit. One moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: While we find that, the exhibit number, General, you had said that the combat unit that was carrying out this training exercise fired on Belanica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that's not what I said. I did not even say that they were carrying out a training exercise, as you said. I did not even say that they were firing at the village of Belanica. Please look at the transcript and see that that is not what happened. There was firing at a plateau sort of close to the village Belanica, but there was no training exercise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood your answer, but we can go back to the document that I wanted to show you, this is P4020, this is the record of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, in -- on page 15 at line 12 your answer is recorded as: "The training exercise was being carried out by the combat group in Dulje. They were carrying out tactical exercises from squad level up to platoon level, perhaps up to company level. That is where this organized training took place." Now you say it wasn't a training exercise. Is there some mistake in the earlier answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I do apologise. This is just one job, one unit, one time-line. The lady said that in Stimlje we were carrying out training exercises and firing at the village of Belanica; that is not interrelated. These are two separate things, and physically it is separate. There's a 15-kilometre distance involved. It does remain that training took place there, a tactical exercise at the level of a reinforced platoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: General, I understand that this combat group that was deployed in the Dulje heights was authorised according to the October agreements, but weren't you under the obligation to notify the KVM before carrying out any type of manoeuvres, for example, a training exercise?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All exercises that take place at a level higher than that of a platoon had to be notified to the KVM.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And in this case - and this is what I was asking you earlier - there was no notification? You did not notify the KVM that you were going to be conducting these operations, these what you call a training exercise?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All this training and exercises up to platoon level we did not send notification on that; from platoon level onwards, we did, through liaison officers, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Can we now have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Perhaps I'm misunderstanding this, and it's important that you clarify just now. The passage I quoted to you a moment ago referred to this exercise I think as being perhaps up to company level. Have I misunderstood that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a platoon, it was not a company. I do apologise. Up to company level is what we were allowed to do in general at brigade level; above company level, we never did anything for several years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm unclear about this, Ms. Kravetz. If you can clarify it, it would be helpful. I would like to know the size of the group that we are discussing and something about the terms of the agreement that applies to it. Perhaps that's already in evidence, but it seems to me quite important.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: General, how many men or what was the size of the combat group that was carrying out a combat -- a training exercise on 15th January 1999? How many men were involved?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You put this question to me, but I cannot give practically an answer because you said training exercise and combat. That's not the same thing. A training exercise is training soldiers in given actions, whereas combat is carrying out combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I know. I maybe misspoke. I'm just speaking about the training exercise, the one that we're concerned with here. How many men were involved in this training exercise that you described in your report?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could not say exactly until I have a look at the report. It's been quite a while, hasn't it, so I cannot tell you the exact number and I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: We can have a look at the report, this is 5D1377. While that is being brought up, do you recall if any vehicles were involved in this training exercise?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that there were vehicles that were used in these exercises, rather, in this training.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What type of vehicles?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, different ones. It was a combination. I cannot say exactly. Combat vehicles, at any rate, that were in that area. They weren't passenger vehicles because soldiers are trained on combat vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So we have the passage there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I think you need to scroll down on the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to read it, General?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm still reading. I haven't finished yet. I've had a look.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now that you've had a chance to look at your report, do you recall how many men were involved in this training exercise? How big was this group involved in the training exercise?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if it pertains to the 15th of January, that date, it is a mechanised platoon on March, and a platoon can be from 27 to 35, 45 men.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And you said that would also include vehicles?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, without vehicles one could not do it really. It has to be combat vehicles, rather, those that are used for training. It doesn't always have to be combat vehicles. Usually there can be a combination, combat vehicles, motor vehicles, depending on whether the training is for one special duty, well, then it's one type of vehicle, either tanks or APCs, or whatever. But if it's several units that are being trained at the same place at a given point in time, then it's a smaller number of vehicles with different VSs, that is to say different military evidentiary specialities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jelic, earlier in this report there is an account of events on the 14th of January, where the training was apparently by a reinforced tank company. You'll see that in the second paragraph. That's a bigger group than the platoon we are talking about; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's a bigger group, a stronger unit that was carrying out training along the route referred to here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How big?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A reinforced tank company, a tank company is around 44, 45 men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what does "reinforced" mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Reinforced means when an additional piece of equipment is added to that unit, regardless of what it is, reconnaissance or a Praga or something, that is the customary term used. It says "reinforced" then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It doesn't refer to additional men being added to the company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it means not only, say, a vehicle, but also the crew accompanying that vehicle or piece of equipment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would the fact that that exercise was to take place out of barracks require to be notified to the KVM?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly, and the KVM was notified of this exercise, that's the 14th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Did this exercise take place on the 15th involve the use of tanks or heavy weaponry?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What it says here is that a mechanised platoon was used. Therefore, a mechanised platoon can be up to three combat vehicles; however, a mechanised platoon can sometimes have minus one/plus one, as we say, that's to say you can take away an APC or add a tank or a Praga or something similar to that. I don't see here that there was anything else except a mechanised platoon in that period of time. I cannot remember myself, but without looking at the entire document I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Can we now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what is a 12.7-millimetre PAM?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On every combat vehicle there is an anti-aircraft machine-gun, 12.7-millimetres, on all combat vehicles, PAM, anti-aircraft machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Could we now look at Exhibit P420.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: General, this is a record, a note, of the meeting that took place the day after the events in Racak, and as you will see on the top of the page among those persons here were Lieutenant-Colonel Petrovic; Brigadier-General Maisonneuve; and the deputy head of the Pristina office Mr. Gilbertson; and an interpreter. If we can scroll down on the page in the B/C/S and on the English, we have General Maisonneuve there who's marked with an M says: "There are tanks and there are artillery outside Stimlje and the artillery is ready to fire towards Dulje, what is up?" And Lieutenant-Colonel Petrovic says: "Normal tasks. "What is 'normal'? "Exercises." And General Maisonneuve says: "Unauthorised move from barracks!" Do you see that, General?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it. Perhaps it can be zoomed in a bit, but I do remember this report presented to me by Lieutenant-Colonel Petrovic. I think it would be best if you looked at the 8th or the 4th of January, 1999. The report of the commission that had toured there, precisely that group, and it says there that weren't any critical remarks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's allow the counsel to ask the questions and you answer the ones that are asked. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: General Maisonneuve testified here and he told the Court that this -- that your unit that was deployed there in the Stimlje area was, in fact, providing fire support for the MUP operation that took place in Racak on 15 January. Isn't that correct, General?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And General Maisonneuve told the Court that several of his teams had observed a tank and Praga on the hills overlooking the village of Racak on the day of the attack, these are VJ, and he said that there were both the VJ and the MUP had been located on the hills overlooking Racak for several weeks prior to the attack. Is that true, General?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you've just said here that they went out a few weeks before and in this document it says one week. This confirms that the units had been there for months, not weeks. The units were at Canovica Brdo, which is to the north-west of Stimlje, which is some 300 or 500 metres altogether, in a wooded area. No superior was provided to the MUP forces by the army during the anti-terrorist action, nor did the army have a plan for any such activity. Even had it wanted to, it could not have done it ad hoc because the MUP forces were already in the village, they had entered in the early morning. I exclude the possibility that the army was in Stimlje.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: But it says so in your report, doesn't it, General, on page 2 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If we're departing from the document on the screen, it should be observed that Petrovic in response to the question whether the move from the barracks was unauthorised claimed that it was authorised. And now we can return to 5D1377.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: On page 2 of your report you say that part of the Combat Group 1 was in the general area of Stimlje, Canovica Brdo where they engaged in regular combat --

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we zoom in here? I can't see.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, we can.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This would be 5D1377. Second page of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Do you see the top of the page where it says that the brigade -- part of the brigade group was in the general area of Stimlje?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: But you just told us that you exclude the possibility that the army was in Stimlje. They were, in fact, carrying out an exercise in the area of Stimlje, weren't they, this combat group?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to explain what this means, the area of the unit. It is marked with three or four points. In the area of the village of Stimlje, or rather, the municipality of Stimlje does not mean in Stimlje; it means in the area of. And that is Canovica Brdo, overlooking Stimlje in a pinewood. Everything else is bare, the ground all around is bare, it's not wooded.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What I don't understand, General, is why if you had been informed that the MUP was going to carry out an anti-terrorist operation of the scale of Racak on 15th January, did you authorise one of your combat groups to carry out training in the vicinity of Racak, in the Stimlje area? Could you explain that?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm trying to explain. On the road from Stimlje towards Crnoljevo, on the left-hand side, that's to the south, there is the village of Racak; and a little more to the north of it, 4 or 5 kilometres away, is Rance, and then there's Crnoljevo and so on. On the opposite side is the municipal village or commune of Stimlje with all the structures in that little town. And we were in the broader general area of Stimlje, that's what it says here, in the general area of Stimlje. So we were physically quite separate, both from the road and from the activities where the MUP was carrying out its activities. It is in the vicinity, but we had been there since April 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: But why did you go ahead with the training exercise when you had been informed that this operation was going to take place in Racak? Why -- is this just coincidental that it happened the exact same day at the time the Racak operation was taking place, is it, General?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you look at combat training, first of all it's not delayed if there's activity going on in the vicinity; there's only increased security and alertness in the unit. One never gives up training unless the unit is attacked or the temperatures are exceptionally low. Training was carried out here, if you see what this is about, combat training, topic 1, observation, monitoring from a combat vehicle by day and by night. This means that you are training soldiers how to observe by day and by night. That is static. You can see that in the first paragraph on page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The truth, General, is that your unit was based in that area and deployed there that morning of 15th January to provide support to the MUP in the operation carried out in Racak; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true. It is only true that the unit was in the area from April 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on to a different topic, General. During your evidence yesterday you said that VJ units under your command participated in a joint action with the MUP in the village of Kotlina on 24 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I just interrupt. I'm sorry I'm a bit slow here, but let me interrupt you just briefly. And can we have the document just back on the screen. It's a simple question, but I need the document back. In the top paragraph, the very first line of your B/C/S version of this exhibit, page 2, it says: "Part of the battle group is in the general area of Stimlje ..." And then in brackets "(Canovica Brdo)." Now, is that another name for Stimlje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Canovica Brdo, "Brdo" means hill; that is a slope stretching in the north-south direction near this little town of Stimlje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This is hill, Canovica Brdo, was not far removed from the area of Racak, was it, General?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's about a kilometre away. They are separated by the road and part of the little town of Stimlje.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: But you could fire from that location in the direction of Racak, the outskirts of Racak, couldn't you, General?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because between this hill, Canovica Brdo, there is a slope on the left-hand side of the Stimlje-Crnoljevo-Dulje road, and from there you cannot see the village of Racak. You can see just a few houses in the distance, some dozens houses, but practically you cannot see the rest because it's protected by that feature which is located between the village of Racak and Canovica hill or Canovica Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If forces, KLA forces, were heading into the village of Racak, they would be passing through this area that was visible from the hill, from Canovica hill; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the road going from Stimlje towards Dulje, the southern part where the village of Racak and the other villages, Malopoljce and so on are located, from there some 500 or 700 metres away or maybe a kilometre away are the foothills of the Jezerska mountains. It's a wooded area, the tracks -- mountain tracks are very rough, and one can only pass through there on foot or with carts perhaps or tractors, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Although you could not see the village of Racak, you could fire tanks or mortar fire in that general direction, couldn't you?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no mortars on those positions. There were tanks and there were 122-millimetres howitzers. Howitzers cannot fire at that range because of their technical features. A tank can fire horizontally up to minus 5 degrees or plus 25 degrees. When it doesn't see the target, it cannot aim. The other vehicles that were there were light mobile vehicles used to escort columns or perhaps defend the area from attack, the area of Canovica hill, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Very well, General. I'll move on. I was putting a question to you earlier. You said -- about the village of Kotlina. You said that VJ units under your command participated in a joint action with the MUP in the village of Kotlina on 24th March 1999. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In one area they were providing support to the MUP forces from the south and west side.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This was an action planned and ordered by you, wasn't it, General?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The action planned for the needs of the army, that was a coincidence. On that day there was an attack on the army, there was a response, and the commander immediately decided what should be done and he put that on a map and issued an order. He drew up the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say the action planned for the needs of the army, that was a coincidence. Which coincidence are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that very day, the most difficult activity had been planned, that is, mobilisation and taking up positions; and that had been planned beforehand. The routing of the terrorist forces had been planned beforehand. However, because of other priority tasks, not all the forces and not all the means were engaged as planned, to rout this terrorist organization.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: But yesterday you said, General, that this action, joint MUP and VJ action that took place in Kotlina on 24th March, was an action that was ordered by you. Do you recall you were shown a copy of the order for this action? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Reduced forces and means were used to carry out this action. The plan was created for the army. We did not create the plan for the MUP; that was done by the MUP forces. All that was done was coordination with the MUP forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: General, you were shown also yesterday a report, it was assigned Exhibit Number IC143, which provided details of this action, including the number of casualties that resulted from this joint operation. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember, I've seen that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: General, the evidence before this Chamber is that a group of approximately 150 soldiers and policemen entered the village of Kotlina, captured a group of around 20 men, beat them, and threw them down to wells on the hills of Kotlina. They later threw explosives down the wells and these persons perished as a result of the explosions. Are you aware of that incident taking place in Kotlina?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that incident from the media and later on following the proceedings at this Tribunal. I had never heard of that before that. My officers and men were not there, so they were not able to give me this information.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: How do you explain, General, that these persons --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm sorry to intervene. It's a very big incident and you are kindly telling us that you -- that the men were not there to inform you, but did you make an inquiry about it, if anything like that was being said? It is a very significant thing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that period it was not a topical issue, it was not generally known, at least in military circles. We did not receive that information from the SUP forces either. We were not informed that something like that had happened. As time went on, there were reports in the media intimating activities by the judiciary, but to this day it is not clear to me how so much of that could be found in that area. Our security organs and our command personnel did not have a single piece of information about this. I made attempts to get more information from the chief of the MUP. He told me that forensic technicians had been sent there and an investigating judge, that they had conducted an investigation and that the legal proceedings would be instituted, but he said that only victims of fighting, casualties in fighting, with the security forces were found. I did not have that information nor did I have any information to pass on to my superior command. It was only information I gleaned in passing. Our military police organs did not go there, nor did our military investigating judge go there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: But -- sorry, General, I apologise bothering you again, but what was the truth about the story? I mean, you belonged to there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the closest to the truth is that in the fighting, because there was a build-up of terrorist forces there. According to our information and from what I heard witnesses of the other side say, there were about 600 to 700 terrorists there. In the combat with those units, which was very fierce and there was a great density of men and weapons, and the percentage of casualties in view of all this was very low. I assume that these were people who lost their lives in the fighting and probably in the combat activities there was collateral damage. So it's possible that somebody who was innocent was also killed as a collateral victim.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: General, there is forensic evidence before this Court that the -- these persons that died on that day died from explosions and their bodies were found inside pits, water-holes, on the side of a slope. You would agree with me, given your experience in the army, that even if these persons had been combatants from the other side, KLA, it is not legitimate to target enemy combatants in this way and dispose of their bodies down a water-hole or a well and blow up the bodies with explosives? That is not a legitimate military action, is it, General?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's bizarre, it's humiliating. For those who do such things, it's incredible. I condemn such actions if anyone did something like that, to kill people, or if they were killed in the fighting, to throw them into pits, if there were such pits - I don't know if there were or not. I think this is inhuman and inhumane, and I truly condemn that regardless of who did it if they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And how do you explain, General, that this inhumane act or action, as you called it, took place in an area where your troops were deployed during the course of an action that you had ordered in Kotlina? How do you explain that, General?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know where my learned friend got this information that the General ordered this action. He gave clear answers in the course of yesterday's examination and he did not confirm that his troops were in the village itself. He explained exactly where they were positioned and what they were doing. I don't want to say anymore to avoid leading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You accept that he ordered the action on the 24th of March?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, we do not accept that, and in my re-direct I will present some evidence to clarify this point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's at page 18980 of the transcript yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry? He's already said today that units under his command participated in a joint action with the MUP in the village of Kotlina on the 24th of March. You can deal with it in reaction if you wish, Mr. Cepic, but there's nothing wrong with the question that's been posed. Please continue, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: General, do I have to repeat my question or can you answer it?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I was asking you -- I'm sorry - how can you explain that such an inhumane act, as you described it, took place in a village, Kotlina, on the day that you were carrying actions -- an action ordered by you with your units and the MUP? How do you explain that such an act took place on that day where your units were deployed?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, my units, as I said, were defending their positions and that was the anti-terrorist action that they carried out. It was defensive because there had been a reduction and the order issued before that was never implemented because there was another priority task which I have already described. Secondly, I was not in charge of that action. We were only defending positions, and it was on that axis that we grouped those forces and means in the direction of the terrorists throughout them. On the other side, on the north side and on the east side, there were MUP forces which entered the village. Who, how, and if this atrocious action took place, if that's how it was, I condemn it; however, it's most likely that those were persons killed in the fighting. Who did what in there I don't know. We did not have our own investigating judge there. It was the MUP that went in there. It was the MUP that brought an investigating judge and forensic technicians to carry out an on-site investigation. I have no reason to disbelieve the judiciary organs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: General, you ordered that action to take place, didn't you, so you were in charge of the action that was taking place in Kotlina on that day, weren't you, General? If you order an action to take place, wouldn't you be the person in charge of such an action?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I ordered my forces which were there in that period to carry out that part. I did not enter the village, and you have that in the reports. I was not in command of the MUP forces. They their own chain of command through the MUP, through the staff, and they agreed with their own. The MUP was not resubordinated to us, it was not under our command, and we could not issue orders to them. As you can see we did not receive reports from them. Had they been resubordinated to us, they would have had to submit reports to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Are you familiar, General, with the area of Kotlina, the geographical area of Kotlina, where it is located?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is south of Kacanik and north, north-west from Djeneral Jankovic in a mountainous area, some 3, 4 kilometres from the main road going from Djeneral Jankovic towards Kacanik.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Kotlina's located in a valley, isn't it, General?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You said your troops were at approximately a kilometre, a kilometre and a half away from the actual town of Kotlina?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The combat group that was there, immediately after approval was given for combat groups to engage in securing the border behind the line, those groups had been there for some months.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Given the layout of Kotlina and the fact that it's situated in a valley, it wouldn't have been necessary for your troops to actually be in the village to be able to observe the men being taken away to the pits and hear the sound of the explosions and see the smoke billowing from these wells or water-holes, wouldn't it, General? It wouldn't have been necessary for them to be in the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know on what basis my learned friend is making this last assertion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, she's making it on the basis that the town is in a valley, and we do know that there's been evidence about the location of these pits and that much can be said about it. We've seen photographs that bear to be the area. The witness is familiar with the area and he can deal with the question. Please continue, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: General, would you answer my question.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, I've said that this area is away from the village. The meaning of the word "Kotlina" is depression; however, the village itself is not in a valley, it's a hilly, mountainous terrain. If you look at the map you will see that it's jagged, rugged terrain with clusters of houses in never more than two, three, four in a group. The village itself is scattered. The unit that was attacked from east and south, the unit that had received approval to engage in anti-terrorist action was able to see always only a part of the village, not even one-fourth of the village, just one small segment. It's rugged, disorganized, unstructured settlement with no access roads, and the peaks are over 1.000 metres. Sometimes through binoculars they would be able to observe part of the houses, but they could certainly not see everything that was going on in the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: But precisely, General, if there are peaks around the village and the village is in a valley and there are large explosions that blew up these around 20 bodies in the wells. This would be something that would be heard anywhere around the village of Kotlina. Even if your units had not had a complete view, they would have been able to hear the explosions; isn't that correct, General?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The units that were located there did not go to observe who is doing what. You have to leave that peak somehow with combat vehicles. You cannot go climbing --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- mountains, you go left and right avoiding obstacles.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That wasn't my question. I was asking if your units, as you say did not enter the village, would they have been able to hear the sounds of the explosions at the water-holes, at these wells where the bodies were blown up. They would have, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if all the vehicles were turned off, if no engines were running, if all the equipment was off, then maybe they would be able to hear it. All the equipment requires the wearing of helmets that protect from excessive noise. If someone was outside not wearing that noise protection helmet, then perhaps they would have been able to hear that kind of sound.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Very well, General. Let's move on. You said in your testimony on Friday that the population of your area of responsibility was moving out of the area mainly due to pressure from the KLA and due to the fact that NATO was trying to create an easier passage for land forces. Do you recall saying that? That's at page 18934 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that. There were more reasons in addition to that, such as financing of the KLA. I would also add that the population was moving out, regardless of ethnicity, towards Macedonia or towards the interior of Serbia. The fear of the NATO aggression was great and people were moving out. If bombs are falling on a daily basis all around your home, it's natural that you would be afraid. People went wherever they had family and some of them even went nowhere into complete uncertainty.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: General, we have heard evidence in this case from General Smiljanic from the air force, who said that the area that was most heavily bombed in Kosovo was the area of the border with Macedonia and Albania. Do you agree with this statement from General Smiljanic?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those two border stretches suffered the fiercest strikes by NATO aviation, and that was not accidental. NATO troops were already in Macedonia and we were expecting a ground invasion. In addition to that, you have the developments along the normal routes used by the terrorist organization from Albania and from Macedonia. If you look at our reports from the 25th of March until the end of May, when the Kumanovo Agreement was signed, there's almost not a single day when a village, town, or barracks were not targeted by air-strikes. I said over 400 projectiles were launched on such a small area, and that was the main cause of migration.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: General, if the population was fleeing due to the NATO bombings, for example, from the municipality of Urosevac, why would they be heading directly where the NATO bombs were falling, which you just said was at the border? Why would they be heading directly in the direction of the bomb? Does that make sense to you?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that does make sense. I didn't mention just Macedonia. People fled also towards the interior of Serbia. They went both south and north --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's leave the interior of Serbia out of it. Just deal with the question about the Macedonian and, indeed, Albanian borders that you've referred to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why would people go in that direction if that's where the bombs were falling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The existing roads, the two existing roads, were not targeted, they were not destroyed. There are four or five bridges there, not a single one was damaged. So it was practical and practicable to use those roads to move out. The only things that were targeted were villages to the left and right of the roads. I'm not simply telling you a story I made up; I'm telling you about the telegrams that went up to the corps command as far as the moving out of people is concerned. As for the rest, it's natural for units to be on first defence lines, and those units were meant to be destroyed and at least removed from the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... I'm just talking about the civilian population. You're saying that they went in the direction of the Macedonian border because the roads had been -- had not been bombed. But wouldn't they be heading directly where the bombs were falling, which is the border with Macedonia? You just told us that was the area that was most heavily bombed. Wouldn't they be heading directly in the direction of fire, of danger?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what? I cannot speak like an amateur, like a dilettante that the border was not targeted as a line. General Smiljanic told you and I'm telling you based on documents that the border belt was targeted, that's a belt up to 10 kilometres deep, that was the main target of the NATO. People used roads that were not destroyed. Bridges were not destroyed, and even before the NATO air-strikes the KLA persuaded people to move out towards Macedonia. At first, before the aggression, they would go from the border to Urosevac, and then during the aggression back. There were cases even during the air-strikes that people went to Macedonia, reached Urosevac, and then after two days of fierce bombing they would go back. They had to run to save their skin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At page 40, line 12, it should read: It's natural for the units to be on first defence lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The truth, General, is that the civilian population of the municipalities of Kacanik and Urosevac were not fleeing because of the NATO bombing or ground attack that was expected; they were fleeing because forces under your command and forces of the MUP were expelling the population. Isn't that true, General?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true. My forces never expelled anyone. They were in their defence areas, and they only responded to direct attacks, except for those who were in the border belt directly. There was no expulsion organized by the army, and I suppose by the MUP either. I can be quite certain that there was none on the part of the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll break now. Again, Mr. Jelic, please go with the usher, and we will resume at 11.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions for this witness at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jelic, a couple of matters you may help me with. Are you familiar to the extent with which Belgrade was bombed?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the information I received during the war through media reports that were very poor because of the destruction of repeaters, Belgrade was struck several times including several vital facilities, beginning with radio television building, several bridges, the Chinese embassy, and the surrounding military installations in the vicinity of Belgrade. I don't have specific data, but I know basically the installations and features that were targeted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you clarify for me what you've described as your brigade's area of responsibility. Just tell me again what that area was during the war?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The area of responsibility of the 243rd Mechanised Brigade was from the front line towards the Republic of Macedonia, its length was 88 kilometres; in the east, from Vitina to Mirosavlje village behind the line; in the west, mount Sar, Nerodimska mountains, Jezerska mountains, and the Dulje pass, that's another 70 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How far inland from -- well, that's the wrong expression. How far into Kosovo from the border did your area of responsibility extend? Just give me the distance rather than the description of the territory.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on the line, around 30 kilometres inland, into the territory of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before the war was your area of responsibility different from the one you've just described?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war our area of responsibility was laid out a bit differently, it was slightly smaller. For instance, from Vitina to Dulje, that was the boundary, it encompassed Urosevac municipality, Strpce, Stimlje, and Kacanik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In places did it then also extend up to 30 kilometres from the bound -- from the border?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, reckoning with the 57th Border Battalion, which before the war was not part of my brigade, it was an element of the corps. But in principle, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you speak of in-depth defence of the border, are you describing your activity throughout the area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In-depth defence is arranged by positions and the units behind the lines in-depth have their own positions and they answer to me, so I'm responsible for the entire condition of units on combat positions in the areas of defence of the respective units, battalions, artillery battalions, that's my responsibility, for the situation in units, their combat-readiness, and their situation, the state of affairs in the area where the unit is located.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In the period prior to the war, what was the maximum extent of the border belt?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The maximum extent of the border belt was 100 metres first before it was increased to 5 kilometres by decision of the federal government. The border belt was extended by decision of the federal government because of the spillover of terrorist forces, smuggling of arms, and various terrorist activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I just want the information I'm asking for at this stage. So the maximum extent or breadth of the border belt was 5 kilometres; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first stage it was 5 kilometres, and it was later extended to 10 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. We've heard various accounts of the difference between the powers of the VJ within the border belt and outwith the border belt. If I can turn now to wartime. Was that distinction, whatever it was, don't go into the detail of it, was the distinction between the powers of the VJ within the border belt and outwith the border belt of any relevance at all after war was declared?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood the question correctly, the powers in the border belt remained the same, the powers of the units in line security and in-depth security remained the same, but these units were merged. The other units have their rights that were envisaged by the rules [as interpreted] in their respective areas of defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So are you suggesting that even after war was declared it was not within the powers of your men outwith the border belt just to stop a civilian and search him?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not have the right to stop civilians on public roads and in public areas outside their areas of defence. If a civilian was found inside areas of defence, they were stopped, their identity was checked, they would be taken into custody, and they were either charged or released. I am saying that the road was an exception. We had no powers there. We had no powers over those two border crossings facing the Republic of Macedonia, namely, the Djeneral Jankovic border crossing and Globocica border crossing. All the rights there belonged to the customs service and the border police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And explain to me again what you mean by the area of defence.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The units that took up positions in their areas, and they are delineated by three points, within that area the equipment and personnel took up the positions there, engineered the positions, created roads, communicating trenches and covers, and prepared for combat and defence from aggression. That is an area of defence, and it is defined for every unit according to their level and on brigade level it is defined for every battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So are you talking of the immediate area around the location of a unit?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The positions of units are arranged in this way. A location from which a possible aggressor is determined. The positions that are engineered have to meet the requirements of the rules of use of every combat piece of equipment, that is, reconnaissance, firing points from which individual fire or group fire is expected, that is an area of defence. It's not static, therefore. It is a line with several positions of cover, and within that area the units have room for manoeuvre. Covers are created for equipment and for personnel, so that they can move from one to another. They can move a vehicle and defend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please excuse my layman's ignorance because I find this concept difficult to understand at the moment. If you take all the areas of defence occupied by your units at any given time, do they completely cover the area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In plains your definition would be correct; in hilly and mountainous areas, like this one, we cover routes of possible movement of the aggressor. We evaluate the layout of the land, the terrain, the forces that are expected, and according to that we deploy personnel and equipment.
