We don't cover the entire area, just the possible routes of movement of the aggressor. They can assume frontal positions, but more usually the positions are flank. We cover the flanks so that there is open space between every two battalions or two artillery battalions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How would a civilian or a group of civilians know whether they were entering a particular area of defence?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An area of defence is a piece of land that is physically secured, guarded. There are patrols and there are ambushes. The patrols would be the first to get into contact with a stray or perhaps organized or unorganized groups of people moving around. There was several cases where people would accidentally run into an area of defence, and we directed them to alternative routes where there is no such prohibition of movement due to the existence of an area of defence. And that happened usually in situations of poor visibility, mainly by night, we redirected them to main roads.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic -- sorry, one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I didn't want to interrupt, page 44, 24, the witness said "Rules of Combat." 44, 24, that were envisaged by the rules, it says here by the rules, but he said Rules of Combat in their respective areas of defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, it's me again. Yesterday you talked about your war diary, you mentioned that this was an auxiliary document. I would be interested in the following. Is a war diary sent to the superior command for supervision and for approval?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all microphones please be switched off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is an auxiliary document and it is used for following the situation in units, and it is kept by the operations organ. So it's not the main operations officer, but the person who is assigned to do that or a duty officer. It is not sent to the brigades and the one from the brigade is not sent to the corps command for approval. It is used primarily to monitor the situation in the respective units. It is an auxiliary document. The basic document in the war is an order, and that has to be on a map graphically and textually presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Are all activities precisely entered into the war diary?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It all depends on the person receiving information, namely, that person is usually on duty all the time, or rather, there are duty shifts at the operations centre in the brigade command and further up. According to the information that this person receives from the field, he makes entries; that is to say, on the basis of what he receives from the field, from the ground. He doesn't check that. So there is a duty officer there, and this is usually unprocessed data, raw data, if we can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, in response to a question put by Ms. Kravetz on the deployment of RMS in the town of Urosevac, what was mentioned was the company of Bosko Cakic. I want to know what RMS means first and foremost?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an abbreviation for war materiel resources, Bosko Cakic is a contractual company that worked on the overhaul of military motor vehicles, not combat vehicles, motor vehicles, and they had their own facilities, their own warehouses with spare parts and workshops, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Wartime materiel resources, what is all of that? You mentioned ammunition yesterday and what does it include in addition to ammunition, this category?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ammunition is the basic resource that is not in the combat vehicle but is kept in the reserves, and the rest is quarter-masters resources, resources of the medical corps, all of that, meaning food and everything else that is necessary for logistics of a unit, even fuel is a wartime materiel resource. If there is an abuse in that period of time, well it -- gasoline was kept at gasoline stations, and they are not in the field, they're by the road, and some fuel is also in fuel trucks on the road as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. When responding to questions put by my learned friend, in view of the responsibility of officers in combat activities, that is to say if they observe that a member of the MUP, for example, or somebody else is in the process of committing a crime, that a military man should stop that. I'm asking you now to the best of your recollection, is this his civic responsibility or is there a special, legal obligation on the part of a military person when this is taking place?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the combat rules what is envisaged is that any kind of criminal offence should be prevented in the sense of serious criminal offences, crimes, then measures and action is taken to punish perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: When talking about civilian facilities, houses and villages from which the terrorists attack the security forces, are they a legitimate military target?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, precisely what Madam Prosecutor said yesterday or asked me about yesterday, that's it. Whoever fires with a weapon, with military equipment, against state organs from any building, regardless of whether it's a school, a house, even a religious facility, that is a legitimate target that has to be destroyed. With all due respect and especially vis-a-vis some facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 5D1337, could I please have that on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, we're going to deal with Racak. So in order to have everything clear to all, we're going to have a map that we've been using so far displayed on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the upper part of the map please be zoomed in. A bit more, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, this is a war map in all fairness, but I believe that you will recognise all the locations here. So I'm going to ask you to use the marker that the usher will give you and first mark the location of Canovica Brdo, where part of your unit was as you described it.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could it be zoomed in a bit more so that I can do it better.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have zoom in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The upper part, please. [In English] A little bit more. Now it's fine I think. One more time, one more time, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, do you need it any more?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can you please put a circle around Canovica Brdo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please move the microphone around so we can hear -- no, no, it needs to come the other way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is it, it's Stimlje and the area of Canovica Brdo is this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please put a circle around the village of Racak.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you please put number 1 by Canovica Brdo and 2 by Racak.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you please put a circle around the town of Stimlje and the main road and mark it by a number 3 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please don't do that. Is it not clear enough, Mr. Cepic --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- without confusing -- you know, the map will get very confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, could you please mark on this map the position of your Combat Group 1 which provided security on the communication route at Dulje. Would you like it to be zoomed in a bit more?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you can't without going back to square 1 on the map, I'm afraid, and starting again. Or is that wrong? Perhaps that --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, if it is feasible from a technical point of view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not possible apparently.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, unfortunately, for the time being this map cannot be zoomed in any further. Could you try to deal with it as it is now. It's pretty small, but try, Dulje, the position of your unit at Dulje.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, could you mark that with a 3, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, from point 3 to point 2, that is to say from the position of Dulje to the village of Racak, what is the distance?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The distance is about 12 or 13 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can we have an IC number for this document, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before we do I want to ask you something about it. The unit that was on its training exercise that you reported on had a position somewhere between the two red circles; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The unit that was carrying out combat training, that's the platoon that we saw in that other exhibit, and before that we saw a company, it was engaged in training in this area, with your permission, here, and in this area that is basically unpopulated because we avoided tank movements and combat training in places where people could be disturbed and also for the sake of the safety of our own units. So it is in these two directions that I marked just now that the training took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just hold on a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One of the things you'll recollect your report said was that part of Battle Group 1 is in the general area of Stimlje, and then in brackets (Canovica Brdo) where they are engaged in regular combat training. It goes on to say: "After combat operations and an attack by Albanian sabotage and terrorist forces started, the unit occupied the sectors and took up the following positions for a flexible defence ..." Now, can you show on the map where these personnel were located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I said about Dulje in relation to a question that was in that exhibit. As for Stimlje, the training of units was in area number 1, as I marked it here, and that is where they conducted that training of observation from combat vehicles, in this area, that's where they were carrying out that training.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And they became -- but their position on the 15th of January was somewhere between the two red circles; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Their positions were here, to the west -- let me mark it, that's where the artillery was, with set-up positions; and that is where they were carrying out training on their own positions, the artillery. The tanks were on this side, on the east, and they were training with their resources. They were not on the move, the units. There was observation from combat vehicles day and night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, what the report says is that: "A 120 howitzer artillery battery was one kilometre south-west of Canovica Brdo and a tank platoon was about one kilometre south-east of Canovica Brdo."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's precisely what I indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, I thought your first red circle was supposed to circle Canovica Brdo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The first circle is Canovica Brdo, that is above Stimlje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But if something is either south-east or south-west, it will be further down the map and either slightly to the right or slightly to the left, which is more or less on the road that runs between Racak and Canovica Brdo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The artillery positions were to the west, or rather, north-west of Stimlje. Canovica Brdo is this part here where the unit was. Canovica Brdo is about a kilometre and a half all the way up to Stimlje itself, and the unit is here, in this area that is the wooded area. And the artillery was to the west of this area for the howitzers and to the right for tanks and APCs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: To clarify the explanation of this, the first markings you made in answer to my questions were in and around the red circle number 1, and then the most recent markings you've made are further north on the map. Now, Mr. Cepic, I understood that the first red circle was supposed to be Canovica Brdo. Have I got that wrong?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the witness pin-pointed the area of Canovica Brdo or Canovica hill, but I can clarify further by asking him questions by your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, he's now said it's further to the north on the map. He's already given answers which don't seem to match. Let's see what the first answer was. "Can you please put a circle around Canovica Brdo," and that's what he did. And this report says -- this report then says that these -- the howitzer battery and the tank platoon were respectively a kilometre south-west of Canovica Brdo and a kilometre south-east of Canovica Brdo. And now it looks as though this is, on the face of what's being drawn, rather confusing. However, please continue if you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you want an IC number for this first of all?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Continue on same document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: New one. Or it would be maybe better if I have a new one, bigger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right, give this one an IC number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be IC145, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can we have a little bit bigger the sector of Stimlje town and Canovica Brdo/hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: One more time, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, the other thing you can do, it's a matter for you, although this may be better, but you could put the IC document back on the screen and you can then magnify it further before you mark anything else on it. Now, either do that or proceed with this one. It's a matter for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I think that would be a little bit more easier if we have the new document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, we have now before us an enlarged map before us. Can you indicate on this map where the units designated in your report -- could you please first circle the area of Canovica Brdo --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please repeat the date of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you give the interpreter the date of the report again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: 17th of January, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, now this evidence is -- well, it contradicts the map, but you'll need to explore that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do you see where it says "Canovica Brdo" on the map? Could you please take a blue marker, General, and mark the positions of the howitzer battery to the south-west of Canovica Brdo.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And the tank, if this is south-east of Canovica Brdo.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've marked it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you please put 1 where the artillery position was and 2 where the tank position was.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: From those positions, can you see the village of Racak directly?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From these positions you cannot see the village of Racak. That's how the units were positioned. In view of this area here between these units and to the south where there is a red circle because of the dense pine forest. Furthermore, there is a steep slope where it says 2 towards Stimlje, it's almost a cliff going down to Kosovska Ravnica that's why -- towards the plain. That's why the tank was positioned facing the plain.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What side were the tanks facing, this plain, where is it?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The plain is to the east of the position in this direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have an IC number for this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC00146, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Now we'll talk about the village of Kotlina, there's been a lot of discussion about that. Could we see document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, just to complete this. Can you tell me why they were located there, Mr. Jelic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This unit which was from Combat Group 1 was located here according to the agreement. Part of that group was located here and this was to provide security for the units going along the Crnoljevska gorge. There was a permanent check-point. If you see this red circle, underneath it there were always three combat vehicles, a reconnaissance or a Praga, escorting the columns moving through Stimlje from Pristina to the Dulje pass and onwards, towards Suva Reka and Prizren. That unit was there, as I said, starting from April 1998. It was part of the combat group which was at Dulje, and the commander of that combat group was at Dulje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you saying every day in life they came out and occupied these positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they had positions, the artillery had its prepared positions, but the positions were taken only if the unit was attacked. However, the artillery was at the positions permanently with a few crew members, but they were always on duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: See, the report says: "After combat operations and an attack by Albanians, the unit occupied the sectors and took up the following positions for a flexible defence ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct. The unit with tanks and personnel carriers was in the pinewoods. As soon as fire was opened, they took up the positions marked here where number 2 is. The artillery had been there for months at these prepared positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm still not understanding you. They were actually for months sitting in these two blue areas marked on the map as number 1 and 2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The artillery was sitting there for months, the artillery. The tanks were inside the pine forest, and only if there was an attack did the tanks move to the positions. All the other vehicles that were there as well as the combat vehicles, there were BRDMs there and Pragas, they had their positions. If the positions were not taken, if they were not escorting a column towards Dulje and Suva Reka, then they were in the area; and whenever there was an attack, they would take up these prepared positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have IC143 on our screens, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, do you see this document shown to you yesterday by my colleague Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it, it's from the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you please read out item 1.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "To the command" --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Only point 1.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On the basis of information gathered in the last three or four days, there has again been gathering and fire by Siptar terrorist forces in the area of the village of Straza, the village of Kotlina, and on the Bojevo-Globocica axis with constant provocation at the repeater on Maja e Salonit hill."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, this fire mentioned here, was it directed at your forces?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what it says here. Part of these terrorist organizations were attacking our facilities which were along the border belt, the repeaters and the units providing in-depth security for the state border.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yesterday we saw an order. Today you explained to us that it was not implemented. Could you please now answer, on the 24th of March, 1998 -- 1999 in Kotlina, did you order any combat tasks to the members of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not issue any combat task to the MUP forces, nor could I have done so, because the MUP was not resubordinated to us. So even had I issued a task, it would not have been valid, they would not have had to obey. I did not issue a single task.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In the course of the war did you issue any tasks to the MUP, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now can you clarify the following, please. If there was an incident, for example, an attack on members of the army in the border belt, and in that incident one or more terrorists was liquidated, so if there was an incident between the members of the army and the terrorists, whose investigating organs would carry out an on-site investigation?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Measures are taken immediately, the military investigating organ is called in with the forensic technicians and the police, and they come and carry out an on-site investigation, and we are responsible for his security and the successful completion of his task so that this can be processed further.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What police?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say "police," I mean our military police, the military police company which was part of my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have 6D501. [In English] Could we have 6D501, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, can you read what it says here. What is this document about?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a little hard to see. It is a cover for a file. The subject is: "Terrorism." The place is: "Kacanik municipality, the village of Kotlina. The date is the 24th of March, 1999, and then it says: "Terrorists."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Will you read the heading?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Republic of Serbia, the Ministry of the Interior, secretariat of interior affairs in Urosevac, group for crime and forensic technology."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the full page in B/C/S, please. [In English] Fourth page, please, in B/C/S. Could we scroll down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you see the last six lines, the last six bullet points?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Where is the weaponry and ammunition seized? Can you read the last six lines.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "General overview of the equipment and weaponry found photographed on the premises of SUP Urosevac. "Part of the weaponry photographed on the premises of Urosevac SUP. "Part of the weaponry and ammunition photographed on the premises of Urosevac SUP. "Part of the equipment photographed on the premises of Urosevac SUP." And then the next line is the same --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Let's not repeat it. Thank you. Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit Number 6D736, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, this document was shown you by my colleague Mr. Ivetic. Could you tell me, who was the primary vehicle, the mainstay, of anti-terrorist combat?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case here it was the MUP forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at 1.2, there is a reference to the PJP company Urosevac. Would you tell me, did you ask these units to be resubordinated?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by virtue of an order that had arrived from the corps command, they should have resubordinated primarily manoeuvring units such as companies should have been resubordinated. These PJP companies of the Urosevac SUP, certainly not buildings, administrations, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you look at paragraph 3.1.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the consumption of weapons and ammunition for that day in the brigade. It says that only one 100-millimetre contact-fuse shell bullet was used; 160, 7.62 --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We can see all that on the screen. Is that the amount expanded for the whole brigade? What are these figures?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you scroll down so we can see the rest? It's my document, but up there in the heading you see it's a report sent to the command of the Pristina Corps about weapons and ammunition used for that day by the brigade. There's the signature of Colonel Kolundzija, Chief of Staff of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We see weapons or artillery PAR S-2M, what is that and what is it used for?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's Strela 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's anti-aircraft weaponry and ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, this is the amount of ammunition used in one day. Is it small, large, could you qualify it.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Relative to the brigade, the amount of weapons, this is a minor number. The brigade did not use more than 0.5 per cent of BK for the whole war, that means 1 to 1.5 shell per tank for the whole duration of the war. I'm using the example of one tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us in a per cent -- the percentage?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 3 to 5 per cent of the combat set for the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit Number P370, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will deal with Dubrava briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have the -- I think that is the -- sixth page. I need the map. Could we have horizontal, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, the position marked "VJ-base," is it correctly depicted?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the area, although we mark it differently, with an ellipsis or a circle but that's the area where the unit was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Are those the static forces, as you described them in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those are the artillery units that were in their position and they were to the north. During the attack by terrorist forces, they blocked the northern they blocked the northern section, that is, to the north of this inscription "VJ- base."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What kind of uniforms did PJP wear during the war?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had new uniforms, dark, brighter green, predominantly green, similar to our camouflage uniforms but with a stronger green colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Ivetic, did you say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I was inquiring of my colleague what part of the cross-examination that is addressed to since I don't recall uniforms coming up at all, at least if it did I must have missed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Based on the document Mr. Ivetic introduced, 6D736, referring to the Urosevac PJP company, I wanted to clarify certain aspects of the event described in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: General, you explained to us what battle order means, what area of responsibility means, you clarified these concepts for the Trial Chamber. What I would like to know is: Outside the area of deployment of your forces, what is the -- which part of the MUP was responsible for public law and order and the personal and property safety of the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the details of the structure of the MUP, but there existed OUPs in Kacanik, Strpce, and Stimlje, those are departments of the interior. Their main staff was in Urosevac. Those units of the MUP were responsible for the entire situation outside of areas of defence of the brigade, just like in peacetime, with the exception of those locations taken up by areas of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You explained that on this main road no bridges were destroyed. Perhaps it would be better to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Sixth page, please. P615, sixth page, please. Could we have horizontal, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you mean this main road going from Kacanik to the south?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I meant this main road going from Urosevac through Kacanik, Djeneral Jankovic border crossing, and on to Skopje.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We have a much clearer picture here than on the map where you put a circle relative to those villages that you said were an obstacle and that many people were killed. Could you just put a circle around that area, those few villages in Kacanik municipality that we mentioned.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's basically this circle, this ellipsis.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And the last question. You said that bridges were not destroyed there. Where any bridges destroyed leading towards Serbia - I mean in Kosovo on the roads towards Serbia?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, from the border of Kosovo and Metohija and further on, all the bridges were destroyed towards Kursumlija, Mitrovica, towards Nis, and Leskovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. That was my last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Could we have just IC number for this document, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be IC147, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jelic, that completes your evidence. Thank you for your patience and for coming to give evidence here. You're now free to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, your next witness is?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Our next witness is Colonel Milutin Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for clarification, my colleagues also suggest it to me, page 66, lines from -- which line? When I mentioned those villages it was related to document which General shown us during the direct examination about the villages and the reasons for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: -- Those events in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just to have reference for that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you now make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You will now be examined by Mr. Cepic on behalf of Mr. Lazarevic. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: For the purposes of the transcript, could you give me your full name.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Milutin Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what is your current status?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Currently I am a pensioner.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me briefly what were the most important positions you held during your career?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In my military career I had the following duties: Commander of the escort battalion -- platoon, commander of a military police company, assistant commander of battalion of the military police, operations officer in a brigade, operations officer in the area zone of the Territorial Defence of Pristina, Chief of Staff of the territorial zone of the municipality of Pristina, commander of the territorial defence of the municipality of Pristina, assistant commander of the Pristina Corps for personnel and housing matters, and that would be it up until the beginning of the aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Once the aggression started, what duties did you perform?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: After the aggression started -- or, to be more accurate, from the 29th of March onwards, in addition to my regular duty through an order of the corps commander, I was appointed leader of a group established by the corps command and temporary commander of the Pristina garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit Number 5D348, please. Could we have in English, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, do you recognise yourself in this document?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I see this document. This document is one of the command of the Pristina Corps dated the 30th of March, 1999. In this document the commander of the Pristina Corps, on the basis of a newly arisen need and with a view to organizing life and work in the Pristina Corps garrison, appointed me leader of a team of the corps command and temporary commander of the Pristina garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm just going to ask you briefly, what were these elements within the group that you headed?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: As can be seen from this order, these elements were the personnel affairs organ; the garrison affairs organ; the department for presenting the situation in air-space; the military band, orchestra; the military prosecutor's office; the military library; and other lesser elements, as stated in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, what were your tasks vis-a-vis the military prosecutor's office and the military court?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: As for the military court and the military prosecutor's office, I, as head of this group, mainly had tasks that were related to securing overall conditions for the life and work of these two important institutions in the corps. Also, for their supplies, for their physical security, and ensuring all other conditions for their normal, lawful work in accordance with the constitution, the Law on the Army, and other regulations that regulate that particular subject matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, did General Lazarevic express an interest in the work of the court and the prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: General Lazarevic, as corps commander, expressed exceptional interest in the work of these two institutions, especially from the point of view of securing the unhindered work of the military court and the military prosecutor's office, which is to say all conditions making it possible for them to work in accordance with the law and regulations. He devoted such attention to this throughout the aggression, and especially when the courthouse was damaged during the bombing and therefore had to be relocated.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, could you or any other officer affect the actual work of the court or the prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, neither I nor any other officer could exercise any influence over the work of the military court and prosecutor's office. The corps commander couldn't do that either or the army commander, and no one else for that matter, because the court and the prosecutor's office were independent institutions and they functioned in accordance with the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, in accordance with the Law on the Army, and in accordance with other regulations regulating the work of military courts and military prosecutor's offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Within your composition in Pristina during the course of the war, did you have any combat units?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Within the group of the command of the garrison of Pristina, or rather, the group of the corps command and the command of the garrison, as can be seen from this order and otherwise, there was not a single combat unit there. All combat units were relocated when the aggression began from the town of Pristina, that is to say those that had been there before, and they took up their positions in keeping with plans that had been made prior to the aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your composition, your units, did they provide security for some facilities or buildings in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Our units did provide security for facilities in Pristina primarily the buildings where they were deployed themselves, or rather, those facilities where these units were for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did members of the army take part in providing security for the house of Ibrahim Rugova?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: No. Members of the army did not take part in securing the house of Ibrahim Rugova.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did your units take part in providing security for the clinical centre and hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The composition that I headed and the composition of the garrison command did not provide security for the clinical centre in Pristina or for the hospital. Most probably this was carried out by people from the hospital security itself or some other structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me what the ethnic composition was of the members of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The ethnic composition of the members of the Pristina Corps was for the most part such that it reflected the ethnic structure of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, or rather, all the ethnicities, nationalities, living in Yugoslavia then were represented.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, witness Lakic Djorovic testified before this Trial Chamber, and he pointed out that in the Pristina Corps there was an officer for supplies in the command of the Pristina Corps, that is, and that his last name was Tijanic. You were the personnel affairs officer. Tell me, when we're talking about this period of 1998 and 1999, was there a person in the Pristina Corps, in the command of the Pristina Corps, with the last name Tijanic?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In the command of the Pristina Corps I worked for a long time in the personnel affairs organ and for a long I'm I was a member of the collegium, too, of the collegium of the commander of the Pristina Corps. And as far as I know, such a person with a last name of Tijanic certainly did not exist in the command of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, is it appropriate time for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It would be. Thank you. Mr. Filipovic, we need to break for lunch now, that will be for an hour. During that period you should have no discussion with anyone at all about the evidence in the case. Just talk about anything else with whoever you meet, but please absolutely no discussion of the evidence. Now, could you leave the courtroom with the usher and we will see you at quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.46 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we have in e-court system Exhibit Number 5D690, please. I think, Your Honour, my assistant checked during the break, and I think we have just a partial translation just for the first page, not for the second one. Second one is not translated. And with your leave I will ask a couple questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, is this your document?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: This document was created in the command of the Pristina Corps, it's dated 28 February 1999, and it was created in the section for personnel, of which I was the chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have the second page, please, horizontal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just note that the second page in fact is a substantive part of this exhibit, and as my colleague has told the Court it has not been translated; and there are a few others that have a similar situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, what do you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this witness is the best-placed to explain this document because it's his, and I believe that his brief explanations would clarify it all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The real question is: Why is it not translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we invested huge efforts to have the documents translated, and we put in a lot of them for translation; but this one is one of the documents on which we were guided by your previous instructions that a partial translation would do. However, of late we are more inclined to be required to provide complete translations. This one is only about numbers, and we can easily read the items, the names of items, in Serbian and the numbers are the same in any language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will admit this one for your charming naivety.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And because I dare say that the bits that are incomprehensible to the Bench at the moment or to the majority of the Bench can be translated, but I repeat, Mr. Cepic, if we really get to something where it's plain that the translation is crucial to proper examination of the witness, we will refuse to admit documents where objection is taken. We've already given you that indication last week. So you have to prioritize your documents according to the timing of the witnesses who will speak to them so that they're available when they're here. For the moment proceed with this one. Just before you do I should have acknowledged when we came on to the bench that Judge Nosworthy had joined us after lunchtime. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, could you please read the title of this document?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: "Survey of manning levels by branch and service," and it concerns professional members of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Would you read the date in the upper right corner, "updated on ..."

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: "Updated on 28th February 1999," that means that this survey provides manning levels of professional members of the corps for this date.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Since we don't have a translation in our system, just give us this first column with the names of categories, infantry, artillery, artillery rocket units of air defence. What is this table?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Having heard your discussion a moment earlier, and for the reasons the Presiding Judge stated, I will read it briefly. This is a survey of manning levels by professional members of service by branch and service. You see the manning levels in the Pristina Corps and the date indicated above. Let me just say what the totals were. The Pristina Corps, by establishment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Stop for a moment. Is there going to be an issue over this, Mr. Sachdeva, because if there is it's no doubt appropriate to go through this, but do you anticipate an issue about the content of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I actually was intending to ask questions generally about manning levels within the corps, but not necessarily with respect to this document; however, as the translation transpires, it may be that I might.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And have you had an opportunity to have an informal translation of these various categories or will you need to obtain that as we go along?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I have had a slight opportunity and I will be able to do it before my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I wonder, Mr. Cepic, what is the value in the witness going through this in detail. If there is something in particular that you want to highlight, then ask him about that, but the document can be read by everyone once it's translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, please be brief. You have the table in front of you. I want the last line, total.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, briefly. From this table we see that the Pristina Corps with its professional members by arms and services was manned to between 50 and 55 per cent of the establishment, which means the corps should have had 4.471 professional members according to establishment, and it actually had 2253 professional members. In this last rubric we see that on that day there were another 270 professional members who were temporarily seconded from other units from outside the corps. That would be briefly the total, and you can see how these numbers were broken down by category and how many men are missing relative to the establishment level, and that's about 50 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: My next question, Colonel. We've heard prior testimony about this but I want to ask you how military conscripts were assigned to various units. Which military occupational specialties exist in the army?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The Pristina Corps, like any other unit in the army, was manned by the peacetime and reserve forces. Depending on the unit there were records kept in the army, records kept in the institutions and agencies of the Ministry of Defence, records kept at the Ministry of the Interior and its various sections, and records kept with employers and other entities related to military conscripts who are assigned there on so-called civic duties or civil duties. There is also a record kept in military territorial bodies covering a number of military conscripts who were not assigned to other institutions and units --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... listened to this for over a minute and learned absolutely nothing. Can we start getting some focused questions, Mr. Cepic, on particular points that you want information on, and please try to control the witness's answer so that the answer actually deals with the meat of the question. We're too far into this case now to have this type of evidence about --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- military conscripts, bearing in mind we've had a great deal of evidence so far about how they are assigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, we want just brief answers. Is it the case that the civilian defence, civilian protection, the Ministry of Defence -- sorry, the Ministry of the Interior had and kept their own separate records of military conscripts?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: As I said, they kept separate records. The Ministry of the Interior had its own record, the Ministry of Defence had its own record --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We know all this already. Please get to something we don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that the next question will be related to something which will [indiscernible] something new. Could we have 5D295, please. Can we have it horizontal, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, what is this table? What is this chart?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: This chart shows us the structure of losses of the Pristina Corps with resubordinated units. In this first circle, this first pie, we see that out of the total losses sustained 27 were dead, wounded were 70, and missing in action were 3 per cent. In the second circle, on the right, we see the structure of those losses broken down by the inflicting force, and we see that losses inflicted by Siptar terrorist forces were 32 per cent, NATO aviation 29 per cent, and ground aggression accounts for 25 per cent of the losses. Other losses equal 14 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. What about the third bottom pie?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: That too is another structure of the losses, this time broken down by soldiers, non-commissioned officers, and officers. We see that out of the total losses of --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, we can see that. We can see the chart. We just needed the basic description from you. Did your own units suffer any losses during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Like many other units in the Pristina Corps, the units that I led sustained losses. We had the following losses: Two dead and three wounded. One of the two dead was an NCO warrant officer Slavisa Izderic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: How were they killed or wounded?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: By Siptar terrorists and NATO air-strikes. Just as an example, Slavisa Izderic was killed by Siptar terrorists and soldier Dejan Ivkovic was killed by a bomb, by a projectile. Out of the three wounded there were two officers and one soldier, they were wounded by Siptar terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did any member of your unit fire a single bullet throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Not a single member of the group of the corps command headed by me and the garrison command fired a single bullet in the course of the aggression, nor did they point a barrel at anyone; we did not have an opportunity to do any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you tell me where in the course of the aggression the command of the Pristina Corps was located, all the places it was located.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The command of the Pristina Corps was located in the course of the aggression by NATO in the general area of the north-eastern part of Pristina, in the area of Grmija, Gracanica, Kisnica, that is the north-eastern parts of Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did it move into the town of Pristina itself later on?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Within this area, the command moved according to need and according to the assessments made to several locations, including the general area of Kisnica, Gracanicko lake, Grmija, and for a brief period it was in Pristina, in the general area of the faculty of law.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was in Hotel Grand?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In the Grand Hotel there was an information centre of the Pristina Corps and the 3rd Army and a place where mail was exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, were you a member of the collegium of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of the collegium of the commander of the Pristina Corps for a long time, until the 29th of March and since that time when -- besides my duty, follow orders, I began to carry out the duty of garrison commander and leader of the group. I occasionally went to briefings and meetings in the corps commander's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was focused on especially at the meetings at the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: At the meetings in the Pristina Corps command and at the collegium meetings, both before and after the aggression, the most frequent topic of discussion were problems of organization concerning the defence of the country and especially emphasis was always laid on respect for the norms of the international law of war and humane treatment of civilians, as well as all other citizens on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. This was emphasised every day at these meetings, and we conveyed that to our subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, what is the significance for you of the 27th of April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I recall that day because it was the statehood day of the FRY, and on that day homage was paid and commendations awarded for fighting against the Siptar terrorists and the NATO aggression to a certain number of members of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Was General Lazarevic present when these commendations were awarded?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, General Lazarevic was present, as was the commander of the 3rd Army, General Pavkovic. It was a Tuesday, I remember, just like today, the 27th and a Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Please tell me whether on that occasion you spoke to General Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: After the commendations were awarded in the lobby of the building of the regional Executive Council where the meeting was held and which was damaged quite severely by bombing, I asked him to visit the units of the command group and the garrison command, and he said that he was busy, that he couldn't do it after the meeting, but that he would do it, time permitting, on the following day. And that's how it came about, that's what happened actually. On the following day, the 28th of April, in the morning, General Lazarevic visited my command, or rather, the place where the part I was in was located, and he also visited another part where the section for the situation in the air-space was located. And later on we went to the Grand Hotel. As I remember, this marked some events on the border, or rather, some humanitarian actions dedicated to the corps units or the border units. I remember that Zaga Pavlovic was there representing the Circle of Serb Sisters. They were a humanitarian organization, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Could you please reply briefly. Were there any urban acts of terrorism in Pristina before the air-strikes began?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In Pristina and its surrounding area, there were many terrorist attacks, that is, attacks by Siptar terrorists, and these attacks for the most part were recorded by the media, many media, and they occurred almost daily.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After the beginning of the aggression, were there still terrorist attacks in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Terrorist attacks by Siptar terrorists continued when the aggression started. I remember many of them, and there are some I don't remember because of the lapse of time. But I remember quite a few such attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can you describe a characteristic example very briefly?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, for example, there was an attack an some Russian journalists carried out just after the beginning of the aggression some three or four days later or two or three days later in the north part of Pristina to the north of Vranjevac. On that occasion two Russian journalists were attacked and their driver from Zemun was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the general area of Pristina, was there an operations zone of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In the general area of Pristina, that is, in the western parts of Pristina municipality, there was an operations zone of the Siptar terrorists called Lab with five terrorist brigades, the 141st, 151st, 2nd, 3rd, and 4th. Two of them threatened Pristina especially, these were 153rd and the 154th Siptar terrorist brigade. They were based in the general area, one in the general area of Kacikol, Kolic, Rimaniste, Makovac and Grastica, and Sicevo. While the other one was in the general area of Mramor, Marevce, Businje, Zlas, Kukavice, and Slivovo. The centre of this previous brigade that I spoke about, the commanders in the village of Grastica near the village of Sicevo, and of the other one in Veliko Zlas near Marevce. The commands of these terrorist brigades were deployed in places where in the course of World War II the ballista organizations were based.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit Number 5D1310, please. 1310, please. I think that we have translation for this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, what does this document show just very briefly?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: As I see, it's a document of the 3rd Army command, security department, dated the 13th of -- I think it says April 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Scroll down document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the third paragraph there's mention of the village of Marevce. Is that the village you have just mentioned as one of the KLA locations?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as I said, this paragraph concerns an eye-witness, who is saying here that 20 Serbian civilians were liquidated in December 1998 by Siptar terrorists in Marevce. That's the general area where this Siptar terrorist brigade was based, relying on that area and logistics from the direction of the villages of Ajvali and Maticane.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have third page in B/C/S and also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I actually would object to the admission of this document into evidence. In the witness's answer, firstly when he spoke about the terrorist groups, the KLA terrorist groups, no time-line, no date was given in his answer, perhaps because none was asked of the witness. Secondly, he has not made -- there's no foundation in terms of his knowledge of this particular incident with respect to the Serb civilians. On what basis is information on that document. I submit that at least these foundational questions should be asked of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think the date was shown in the document, was it not, of December 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President. However, when my learned friend initially asked the witness of questions related to the Albanian terrorists, no time-line was given and no date was given by the witness. In fact, I understood the answer to refer to the time when NATO started the bombing campaign. That can be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, can you deal with the timing of this and also the basis of the witness's knowledge of these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, when did you learn about the terrorist acts?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I learned about these terrorist acts before the aggression and from the point of view of the duty I was holding and also the point of view of a citizen, because in that area in December and before December 1998, many citizens of Serb ethnicity went missing from the villages of Slivovo and the villages in Novo Brdo municipality, in the vicinity of Marevce. The missing were never found, and one can see from this document that they were killed, they were liquidated.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is this document, Mr. Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a document, as can be seen, from the security department where an eye-witness is saying that he was an eye-witness to the shooting of these 20 Serbs. And I had learned before that in that area in the general area of Marevce many Serbs had gone missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When did you receive this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw this document during my proofing with the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So this isn't a document that came through your hands in the course of your official duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not see this document when I was performing my duty, but I know about those people who were killed -- rather, I know that they had gone missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. And which was the paragraph that dealt with the --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why are we on this page?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: First page -- I have some questions relating to 11th paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's go back, please, to the first page. What's your position now on this document, Mr. Sachdeva?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I must persist in my objection. The witness has now told the Court that he has learned from this document itself that the Serb civilians were liquidated, allegedly liquidated, and he would have no basis to demonstrate that the Serbs that he was talking about went missing are, indeed, these Serbs that have allegedly been liquidated. Secondly, as the witness has told the Court this is not a document seen prior to proofing. It's from an organization or from the 3rd Army of which he was not a specific member of, albeit the 3rd Army was in the chain of command. And therefore, I persist in my objection that that has not been a proper foundation for this to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, this document has already been admitted, or rather, it was on the 13th of November, 2007, that it was admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Through which witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I think with General Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In these circumstances all we can do is give appropriate weight to what the witness has said about these events in light of the source of his knowledge and bear in mind the comments you have made, which do seem to have some force and could lead to us - could lead to us - having no regard to what he said about the relationship between this document and the other event that he was speaking about. We would have to evaluate the potential link between the two in the light of all the evidence we hear in the case. So please continue, Mr. Cepic. It's unlikely that referring this witness to paragraph 11 is going to assist you in any way. You would be far better asking for his own personal knowledge of matters --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- bearing in mind this document has nothing to do with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, where were you born and where did you spend most of your life?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was born in Pristina. I finished most of my education in Pristina, in Ajvalija, Gracanica, all of that is nearby, near this locality where these persons were liquidated. Nearby I have friends, I have relatives that I talked to when their fellow citizens went missing, especially from the village of Slivovo and from the villages that are in the northern part of Marevce in the territory of the municipality of Novo Brdo. All of these missing persons were never found.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. As for your knowledge that you refer to just now, does that correspond to the documents that are in this case?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: They fully correspond --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, whoa, please, please. Are you now going to invite a witness who's looked at documents in proofing to tell us about the correspondence between his recollection and the documents in a very general way? Is that what you intend to do? Because if you do, it will not assist us in any way. If you have got to for some reason put a document to him to establish the identity of what's in the document to his -- to his knowledge, it's very likely the question will have such a leading content as to be valueless to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you, Your Honour. I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, the town of Pristina itself, was it bombed during the aggression?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The town of Pristina and the surrounding area were bombed during the NATO aggression on a daily basis. The bombings took place day and night.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, Prosecution witness Emin Kabashi in his statement claims that NATO never bombed before 1800 hours. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Such a claim, quite simply, is not correct. Pristina as a town and the surrounding area, as I've already said, were bombed every day, day and night, in the morning, midday, evening, public holidays, Saturdays, Sundays, on Easter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have in e-court system Exhibit Number 5D241. Could we have in B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 1.1, the second bullet point, 1.1 second bullet point starts with the following words: "1445 hours - two explosions in Dragodan" --

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Dragodan is a neighbourhood of Pristina that is in the western part of town viewed in relation to the centre of Pristina. And here we can see that at 1445 hours there were two explosions in that neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the connection -- your connection to this document, Mr. Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, my connection to this document is from the aggression period because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- In relation to my command post the operations centre of civilian protection was close to it and I regularly received information from them about the areas that were bombed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So is this a report to you, albeit it says the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. This report was not submitted to me, but it was submitted by the operations centre of the civil protection, and they had this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That may be. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the link between the witness and the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: This document is from Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, and what's his link to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: He was the member of Pristina Corps also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Dealing with this issue? Is this his report or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: It is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So why did you ask him about this, apart from showing that this document says that bombing took place before 1800 hours, which he's already told us? What was the purpose of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- What was the purpose of showing this document to him? So I can see if we are doing anything productive here or simply wasting time. I mean, the document exists, it says what it says --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Okay, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- He's got no familiarity with it, He hasn't told us that he was there and saw the bombing take place and can confirm it. So we haven't advanced matters by actually spending time in court in exploring this orally. Do you understand? We're keen that you use this time for things that need to be dealt with orally, and you undoubtedly have so far in your case, both you and Mr. Bakrac, presented a great deal of evidence that had to be done orally, it's obvious, because it was controversial in dealing with issues that have already been explored in the Prosecution case. It was particularly important to deal with that orally. But I, speaking for myself, doubt if anything that Mr. Filipovic has said could not have been said in a written statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will speed up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm sorry, but does that mean that the document will not be into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I suspect it's already -- is this already admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: This is already in the system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You see the --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just to check one more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Our records show it has not been, that's why I rose.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not been admitted earlier, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And there may be other ways of doing it, from the bar table or through other witnesses, but this is not the way to deal with this sort of material and secure its admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Microphone not activated] Just to start microphone. Could we have Exhibit Number 5D1242, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, are you perhaps familiar with this footage?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
