utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with this footage; they are from the night between the 6th and 7th of April, 1999. It was sometime after midnight. The city centre, nucleus, of Pristina was bombed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was bombed specifically on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, the main post office in the centre of Pristina was hit, also the provincial institution for social welfare, and many buildings that were in the immediate vicinity of these two buildings, and those were residential buildings. Other buildings in the area were seriously damaged, namely, the Provincial Council of Kosovo, the national bank, Investbanka, the Municipal Assembly of Pristina, and some residential buildings where citizens of Pristina lived were totally destroyed and burned down. There was over ten casualties among the civilians and over 20 civilians were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the second part of the same document, or rather, of this material.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid that we have a technical problem, that we've skipped a part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, you want an earlier part, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's go back to where it should be. Is this the right part?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I hope, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is what we saw already.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- Something. I think that we solved it in a short time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, you described this incident to us. My question is the following: Were you there on the spot that night?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: That night I went out and I was there on the actual spot where this happened, because my command was a few hundred metres away from this particular spot. The scenes were terrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do you know the names of some of the victims?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I know many of these victims because members of my command together with me tried to help and get the dead and wounded out of the rubble. In addition to the civilian protection that participated in this, members of the command group, or rather, the garrison command took part as well. Many dead persons were taken out of the rubble, both Siptars and Serbs and Turks --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you going to give us the names of those that perished?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Example Ali Rexha was seriously wounded and his wife Ikbala Rexha, she was rescued from the rubble but by the members of my command and Cedomir Ilic. Kedzi Omer's wife was seriously wounded. He worked in TV Pristina and her mother, too, Sajrana and many others. The houses were totally destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Is it the case that an entire family was wiped out in the bombing?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, a whole family was killed, but some families escaped -- had a very narrow escape, such as the family Denda, whose house was razed to the ground, and they had left just two days earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, just tell us briefly whether any other examples of the army extending assistance to civilians specifically by your unit?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Many, indeed. Just one more example.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Near our command, because we were located in the centre in a briefer building near the Municipal Assembly building, a Siptar woman with a wounded child was passing by, conscript Nebojsa Dukic ran to her aid. He together with Dejan Vitorovic took a service vehicle that had been requisitioned from telecom, drove the child and mother to the Pristina hospital, where they were assisted medically.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you report these humanitarian actions to the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: At the briefings in the office of the corps commander, I emphasised such examples, and General Lazarevic always commended people for that and insisted that they should go on in the same spirit and that we should convey that to all our subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I've already mentioned a Prosecution witness Emin Kabashi, who said in his evidence, in his statement, that in end March when the aggression started at Vranjevac bridge he saw a tank, next to that tank there were persons who stopped civilians, intercepted civilians, and divided them into two groups. My first question is: Do you know where this bridge is; and second, were there any tanks in Pristina during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I know the Vranjevac neighbourhood and where that bridge is, it is in fact a fly-over, looks like a bridge, crossing a railroad on the Pristina-Podujevo road in the very neighbourhood of Vranjevac. That's the answer to the first part of your question. As for the second, from the start of the aggression until the end, not a single combat unit was deployed there, especially not with a tank, because the 15th Armoured Brigade on the very eve of aggression left the town of Pristina and took up positions that had been planned for it outside of Pristina and from that time on there were no tanks in Pristina, especially not near this fly-over, which is very narrow, and where it would have been a sitting duck for NATO aeroplanes and Siptar terrorists who were numerous in Vranjevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, we had another witness, another Prosecution witness, Ms. Nazlie Bala. She claims that Pristina town on the 26th of March, 1999, was blocked and there were members of the army, the MUP, and Serbian civilians standing on all access roads. The roadblocks were made of barbed wire and Albanians were not allowed to move within the town of Pristina at all. That is her assertion.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: There are many lies in all that. It simply isn't true. Pristina was not blocked, either by the army or anyone else. Barbed wire is a total fabrication and nonsense. There was no barbed wire anywhere inside or near Pristina. There were many foreign reporters criss-crossing this area who can confirm this and many citizens who could see it with their own eyes, as could I. That is absolutely not true. There were no roadblocks and no barbed wire, nor was the population prevented from moving around on their own business and errands.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, you were born in Pristina. Could you please respond to this claim by the same witness. In her statement P2262, she claims that she lived in Lapi Street 30. What is this street? What does it mean, Lapi? Do you know of that street?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: She must have meant Lapska Street because Lapi is Albanian. It should be Lapska Street 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. She stated that 30 Lapska Street in her supplemental statement, her house was very close to the centre of Pristina near the old market on a hill from which she had a good view. Could you say anything about these directions?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: It's a relative thing what is close to the centre or not, but Lapska I would say is relatively far from the centre. It's closer to the suburbs of Pristina and closer to Vranjevac neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have in e-court system Exhibit Number P615, page 30, please. Actually, 31, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, we see before us a map of Pristina. Could you show us where the centre is, where the old market is, and then Lapska Street, 30 Lapska Street. Could you put a circle around each of the locations, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... please. Just zoom in, please. Now it is too big. Zoom out, please. Zoom out, please. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the aggression there were two functioning markets in Pristina, that is, before the aggression. During the aggression one of these markets was closed. So out of these two, none of these two are the old market. The old market was close to the cinema called Omladina and the Executive Council of Kosovo, right next to the destroyed post office building. This map is not quite clear for this kind of work, but let me say -- I'm not sure I marked this correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you put a circle around it and number 1.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: But it was next to the destroyed post office building, 20 metres behind the post office building.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you please put number 1 there.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Now, please, show us Lapi or Lapska Street.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Lapska Street should be here, in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Put number 2.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What is the distance between these two points?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: 1500 metres I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have IC number, please, for this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC148, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, the same witness claimed that from the roof-top of her building she saw, among other things, Kojlovica village. Is it possible to see Kojlovica village from this position?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Kojlovica is one of the smaller villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just tell us, is it visible?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: From this point, Kojlovica village could not be seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. She goes on to say that from her roof at 30 Lapska Street she saw the Serbian artillery firing from a position in Vranjevac towards Kojlovica village. Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: It's not possible for more than one reason. First, the Serbian artillery, that is, the artillery of the army, was never located in Vranjevac. It wasn't located there and it couldn't have been located there for tactical reasons because there's almost no street in Vranjevac wider than 2 meters [Realtime transcript read in error "kilometers]. Vranjevac was a major logistical base for the terrorists, and the second reason is that not being there they were not able to fire from there, especially not in the direction of Kojlovica village, and even if they had fired, if they could have fired, they would never have used artillery against civilians, especially since Kojlovica is a mixed village populated by both Serbs and Albanians --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In transcript actually page 98, line 22, not 2 kilometres, 2 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The same witness, Colonel, claims that on the 28th of March, 1999, she heard shooting in Vranjevac, she heard gun-fire. What could you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear which day.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: 28th March 1999.

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: She could be right there. On that day there was shooting in the broader area of Vranjevac because the terrorists relying on the support from Vranjevac attacked the Russian journalists I mentioned earlier. That's the occasion when that driver from Zemun was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Let's just clarify something, General. The members of the army, what kind of uniforms did they wear?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: It is the generally known fact, they wore the uniforms prescribed for the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, was anybody moving out of Pristina?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: People were moving out of Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: When did that first start?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: It started on the very eve of the aggression, and then, to a lesser or greater degree, it continued during the aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did anyone move out in October 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In October 1998 and later, in September and November, people did move out of Pristina. I know that some humanitarian -- humanitarian organizes like the UNHCR in particular, a number of citizens of Serb ethnicity were contacted and directed to move from Pristina. Many Serb citizens moved out of Pristina then, especially the category of refugees that had come from Croatia and Bosnia to live in Pristina. These were entire families that were moved under the auspices of these organizations, without passports, and they didn't even have to pay their own expenses. They were primarily moved to the United States of America. I know entire families and I know their names and surnames, and I know quite a few of these people personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before the bombing started, what was the situation like? Were people moving out then, on the eve of the bombing?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On the eve of the bombing a number of citizens moved out of Siptar and Serb ethnicity and of other ethnic backgrounds because of this objective fear from bombing. Because in foreign media in particular, a lot was being written about bombing and citizens of Serb and Siptar ethnicity were moving out, especially those who were better off. Some of them moved out on the very day of the bombing, or rather, just before the bombing started. For example, an entire building, the so-called Devet Jugovica building in a particular neighbourhood in Pristina, in Tranije Street. They moved out and it was mainly retired military personnel who lived there, ethnic Serbs and Siptars, and a small number of active of duty members of the military. So practically all the people who lived in that apartment building moved out before the bombing started. Only the family of Colonel Cedomir Nikolic and Dzaklic Zivojin stayed on in that building. The families of retired Colonel Suljo Ajeti and Cehaja Ramadan moved out and Dr. Ljubica Azemi and many others who lived in that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the members of the army and police move their own families out due to fear?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: A number of members of the Army of Yugoslavia and a number of members, or rather, families of members of the Ministry of the Interior, like many other citizens, moved out parts of their families, especially their children, on the eve of the bombing. That is a well-known fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What was the reason for all these moves?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: All these moves before the aggression were due to the real threat of bombing, especially because of what was learned from the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And were propaganda calls made to leave Pristina?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: During the aggression, propaganda calls were sent out to leave Pristina, some propaganda calls were made with a view to intimidate the population and the members of the army and the members of the Ministry of the Interior. Such leaflets were distributed during the course of the war in Pristina and the surrounding area. These leaflets were dropped from aircraft too.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could we have 5D1364, please. Unfortunately we have no translation for this document, but with your leave just a brief question. [Interpretation] The document is in the Albanian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, what does this document represent?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document -- or actually a leaflet, or rather, propaganda material that could often be seen during the aggression in the streets of Pristina. You cannot see it now on the screens. I remember because I had it in my hands, it was identical in the original too but it was red.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What does this leaflet ask for?

utterances.speaker: MILUTIN FILIPOVIC
utterances.text: This leaflet is in the Siptar language. Citizens are called upon in this leaflet to leave, the Siptars, that is, to leave Kosovo and Metohija; namely, to move out in the direction of Macedonia and in the direction of Albania. And before a major Serb offensive the KLA is not in a position to protect them, and due to this offensive, alleged offensive of the Serb forces, they should move in these directions from Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When did you first see this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I first personally saw this document in the streets of Pristina sometime during the first half of the aggression. I don't remember the exact date. Later on, one of my officers Dobrivoje Stojanovic gave me an identical leaflet later because he found it in town because there was this procedure involving propaganda material. If it had been issued by the General Staff a lot before the aggression and it is in line with that, that this officer handed over this leaflet to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This particular one that we are looking at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you give it to Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I gave it to Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And does it look genuine to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not only that it looks genuine to me. I had a document with this content in my own hands. Everything is the same but it's red.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand what you're saying about an actual document, but does it make sense to you for there to be a link in a document like this between the KLA and Rugova?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I did not go into such an analysis, but bearing in mind --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, could you do it now. Could you tell me if a makes sense in a document to link these two.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It does make sense. It depends on the author. It depends on who the author is, and it is certain that the Siptar terrorist organizations and their centres are the author.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So are you saying that people in Albania -- sorry, people in Kosovo were not aware of the actual relationship between Rugova and the KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, whether they were aware or not is something that I cannot confirm. However, ordinary people could be misled by this leaflet. Very few ordinary people went into this kind of high-brow analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So how do you say they would be misled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If hundreds of such leaflets are found in different neighbourhoods every day where citizens live, it is quite certain that one could expect a number of them to be misled by that in this direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you use the word "Siptar," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's not only on this occasion but also in relation to what I testified about until now. When I say "Siptar" in the context of what I'm saying here today, I mean, first and foremost, the Siptar terrorist forces, not taking into account the other Siptars who were loyal citizens of the Republic of Serbia and Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'd like to know what you regard as the meaning of the word "Siptar."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the meaning of Siptar is the same like Serb, it is national or ethnic affiliation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there no Serb word for "Albanian"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serb word for Albanian in Kosovo and Metohija, the most frequently used one was Siptar, and that was due to several reasons, particularly because they called themselves that. Even the Albanology institute in Pristina issued a dictionary "Fjaloni Serbisht Shqip," which is to say a Siptar-Serbian dictionary. I personally got a dictionary, that dictionary from Fazli Sulja the director of that institute, he was a professor of mine, Dr. Fazli Sulja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In Albanian, Mr. Filipovic, does Siptar not mean Albanian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Albanian, Siptar can be Albanian or Siptar, but we know it's Siptar. It's the name that they use to denote themselves, and there's absolutely no problem about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's what I'm trying to understand. Is Siptar not the Albanian word for Albanian, or am I misunderstanding the language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Siptar is the word commonly in use by the population in Kosovo and the population in Albania, but let me stay away from Albania. That's the word used by people in Kosovo, the Siptar population of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We obviously don't really understand each other. Please continue, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry -- I'm sorry, I'm very sorry, forgive me for this. How does this leaflet come into your possession, this leaflet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had such leaflets in my hands before, before this one, I destroyed the early ones. I was given this particular one by one of my COs from the garrison command, Dobrivoje Stojanovic, it's a leaflet he found lying around during the aggression. I had many others that I destroyed but I didn't destroy this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: When you talk of many others, you mean facsimile, similar type, or you mean with a different subject?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Like this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: You also said that these were found in some neighbourhoods. When you speak of those neighbourhoods, were these neighbourhoods of people you call as Siptars or is it a mixed neighbourhood? Were these mixed neighbourhoods?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mainly in neighbourhoods with a predominant Siptar population, but a leaflet has a name in Serbian that includes the word "to fly," a leaflet flies easily, it can fly over from one neighbourhood to another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: And it's my understanding that this word, "Siptar," is actually a derogatory word for the Albanians. Am I right or am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with all due respect, it is not true, it is not correct, it is not a derogatory word, it is not a word meant to denigrate; it's a word commonly in use in Kosovo and Metohija, it's a word featuring in textbooks that are printed in various institutions, scientific and research institutions, academic institutions, including the university and the institute of Abanological studies. I told you a moment ago that a dictionary, a Serb-Albanian dictionary, was published before the aggression, Serbian-Albanian dictionary at a time when the director of that institute was Dr. Fazli Sulja --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: But you see there are many words which are used and are in dictionary, but everybody understands that they are being used in the sense of derogation, like for the black the word was "negro" and so on and so forth. Is it the same sort of thing used by people who didn't like the other side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- this is certainly nothing like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Some documents saying derogatory, Siptar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you can certainly not place it in the same context as the word "negro" as used to denote blacks, it's not a derogatory word. It is the word that most of the Siptar population used to denote themselves. Why would we use another word than the word used by the majority of the Siptar population themselves?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: But in many of the official documents we found the word used and the explanation that this is derogatory for this. Didn't we see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you can make all sorts of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... because it's the comment of a translator and not something we're taking account of. But your last question -- your question to Judge Chowhan I don't understand. You say: Why would we use another word than the word used by the majority of the Siptar population. What I don't understand is why you don't call them Albanski since that is the Serb word for Albanian just like an English-speaking person would call you a Serb. We wouldn't call you the word that you might use to call yourself. That's the bit I'm trying to understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I tried to say this nicely. There is no problem. We can call them Albanian or Siptar, it is no obstacle between people. I told you I used that word because most of the people of that ethnicity use it to call themselves. Now, it's another matter how elitist circles might interpret that. As far as I'm concerned, there's no problem in using either word, no formal and no practical problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: If I might, and I feel qualified to speak in this matter, I believe that the word that blacks find offensive is "nigger" insofar as "negro" by definition is abrasive, it would not necessarily be considered offensive, although it's not usually used nowadays. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, is there anything else you want to deal with before we adjourn?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Tomorrow morning I will raise all my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You'll be here on your own then.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Really -- probably. With your leave, if we can leave the courtroom, that will be fine for all parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Since we'll be sitting tomorrow afternoon. We've done our best to change that, but it's not possible, I'm afraid, tomorrow. We must break there, Mr. Filipovic, for this evening and we will resume your evidence tomorrow, and that will be at 2.15. So you need to be back, ready to commence evidence, at 2.15. Meanwhile, please have no discussion with anyone at all about the evidence in this case. Now could you please leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 28th day of November, 2007, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.35 p.m.,
